item.title: Three Faces of the Moon over Kitt Peak
item.description:
On 3 March 2026, the Moon showed us three of its “faces”: the full Moon, the blood Moon, and the distorted Moon. This image compares these views as seen from the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO) in Arizona, a Program of NSF NOIRLab.

When full, the Moon is completely illuminated by the Sun. The full Moon appears on the left of the image, taken at 1:12 a.m., before the start of the eclipse.

The center image depicts the fully eclipsed Moon. Taken later at 4:33 a.m., the full Moon is mostly within Earth’s umbra, the darkest part of its shadow. The sunlight that reaches the Moon inside the Earth’s shadow must first pass through Earth’s atmosphere, which covers the Moon in red light instead of the usual white sunlight. The right side of the Moon in this image lies within Earth's penumbra, the outer and lighter part of Earth's shadow. Within the penumbra, only a portion of the Sun's light is blocked. Because of this, the Moon appears only slightly dimmer and does not take on the deep red color seen during a total lunar eclipse. 

After a day of sunshine, the Moon was captured in the right image at 6:59 p.m., low over the horizon. As its reflected sunlight traveled through Earth's atmosphere on its way to the observer, atmospheric refraction distorted the Moon's shape and dispersed the light, subtly separating it into different colors. In this instance, the distortion created an optical phenomenon in which the upper rim appeared green, and the lower rim appeared red. Though the green rim is often too thin to be visible, it can be seen under the right conditions, like in this image.

You can find an unannotated version of this image here.

Petr Horálek, the photographer, is a NOIRLab Audiovisual Ambassador.

item.title: Mid-70s Spring in the Sonoran Desert
item.description:
Winter rains awakened this lush field of California poppies near U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO), a Program of NSF NOIRLab. Carey Portnoy, a former Technical Assistant at Kitt Peak, captured this image sometime between 1975 and 1977. This area along Arizona State Route 86 is known for its abundance of springtime wildflowers, but it is full of interesting desert flora year-round. Common plants that can be spotted on the drive up to Kitt Peak include saguaro cacti, jumping cholla cacti, and manzanita bushes (which give the mountain its O’odham name, l'oligam Du'ag, or Manzanita Shrub Mountain). Astronomers are honored to be permitted to conduct scientific research on the sacred mountain located in the homelands of the Schuk Toak District within the Tohono O’odham Nation. 

Standing tall on the mountaintop in the distance is the eighteen-story-tall NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope, which can be seen from over 50 miles away. At the time this photo was captured, the Mayall was just beginning to study the cosmos. It was the second-biggest telescope in the world at its first light in 1973. The Mayall telescope currently hosts the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), the world's most powerful multi-object survey spectrograph. DESI is supported by the U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science.

If you’ve captured an amazing photo of any NSF NOIRLab Programs or facilities, we might feature it as a NOIRLab Image of the Week. You can submit them for consideration to comms@noirlab.edu or info@noirlab.edu.

item.title: Comet C/2025 K1 Caught in Color!
item.description:
The shattered remains of comet C/2025 K1 appear in color in this 2025 image from Gemini North. Gemini North is one half of the International Gemini Observatory, supported in part by the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) and operated by NSF NOIRLab.

This color image of comet C/2025 K1 was taken on 24 December 2025, following earlier observations from 11 November and 6 December 2025. This comet has been capturing astronomers' attention in part because it originated in the distant Oort cloud and in part because it is breaking into pieces. Earlier observations showed that the comet had broken into a parent body and four fragments, but this new image reveals that the fourth piece appears to have dissipated. When comets break apart, the smaller chunks shed mass and leave behind a cloud of gas and dust rather than a solid body. This is what happened to the dissipated fragment of comet C/2025 K1. This full-color image also helps researchers understand the comet's composition. Due to its color, researchers suspect that the fragmentation of the comet C/2025 K1 exposed fresh ice on the surface.

Two fragments here are clearly separated from the parent body by about 3 arcsec and 13 arcsec (2,300 km and 10,000 km). Bryce Bolin, a research scientist at Eureka Scientific, and his colleagues Carl Ingebretsen and Meredith MacGregor of Johns Hopkins University chronicle the evolution of the comet's fragments and colors throughout December 2025 in a paper under review at The Astronomical Journal.
